items.title: A novelist is back on the cover of TIME.
items.summary:
Today, TIME Magazine  has published their list of 100 “must-read” books of 2026 , including  Yesteryear   by Caro Claire Burke, who is also featured on the magazine’s cover.

The last novelist to be featured on the cover of TIME was Taylor Jenkins Reid , in 2025; before that there hadn’t been a novelist on the cover since Akwaeke Emezi was featured as part of the magazine’s “Next Generation Leaders” package in 2021 (Amanda Gorman was also featured in a solo cover that year). Novelists used to show up in this spot all the time, but they have rather fallen off in the magazine’s modern history. In 2010, Jonathan Franzen famously became the first living novelist to be featured on the cover of TIME  in a decade, followed by Colson Whitehead, in 2019 . So at least things are picking up this decade.

See Caro Claire Burke’s cover below, and read the cover story here . (You can also read Lit Hub’s interview with Burke here .)

Photograph by Tonje Thilesen for TIME @tonjethilesen

items.title: And the Best Literary TV Adaptation of All Time is…
items.summary:
After six rounds of voting , we’ve got a winner. Choppering in to claim their prize after squeaking past Roots, it’s…

M*A*S*H 

The anti-war workplace dramedy is your top literary TV adaptation. It feels fitting that a show from our Cozy category won this thing, since dependable and comforting is television’s best, and truest, mode. The black comedy of the Robert Altman film and the dizzying highs and lows of combat medicine in Richard Hooker’s book found their most enduring expression on CBS. For 11 seasons and 256 episodes, M*A*S*H evolved from a straight-ahead sitcom into something more dramatic and challenging—the shift in laugh track is just one example of how the show began to take its stories more seriously.

And it was beloved. The 1983 finale still holds the record for the highest percentage of TV sets watching the same program simultaneously. And I’m not sure that it’s true, but I love the story about New York’s toilets breaking after the finale: apparently so many people waited until the very end of the two and a half hour episode to pee, that when everyone went all at once, it overwhelmed the city’s plumbing.

What other TV show was so popular that it broke a city’s toilets? Only  M*A*S*H. 

Thanks for playing along with us! Now I retire to my Bracket Cave deep in the hills, to rest and to dream of what brackets may come.

–James Folta

items.title: Nafissa Thompson-Spires’ Debut Novel Satirizes the Idea That Black Men Are Invincible
items.summary:
Rumor has it that now—in our world of alternative facts, of journalists replaced by influencers, experts replaced by AI, and of news constantly deemed fake—we’ve finally, finally done away with that dastardly thing called “truth.” Hard data is tough to come by, since sensationalism’s better for algorithms. It’s difficult to tell if any given video is secretly an ad. Not even our Google searches can be trusted. They’re calling it a “post-truth society,” and here we are, left in constant skepticism over the fabric of our reality. Did we really have a White House Press Secretary between October 12th and October 16th, 2026? Is Manon of KATSEYE really on “hiatus”? Could we really “see everything”? Ugh. We can’t even trust our documentaries anymore.

Multi-award-winning, National Book Award longlisted author Nafissa Thompson-Spires knows none of this is new. Her second book and debut novel, The Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milford (a current First Novel Prize finalist) is set in the all-Black town of 1920s Newville, where the town has finally, finally done away with that dastardly thing called “Richard Milford.” An infamous moonshiner, an unloyal womanizer, and just plain mean, the town will tell you—collectively—that this is good riddance. That is, except for his four wives and his beloved housekeeper Alberta. They’d surely remember him differently, right? Unless they somehow had reason to kill him . . . Wait, how many times did Rich die?

With slick wit, a wry sense of dark humor, and a hefty dose of whimsy, Thompson-Spires deconstructs the idea of truth before our…

items.title: The Best Debut Novel of the Century So Far
items.summary:
We always knew y’all had good taste, and you confirmed it when you selected Homegoing for the first listeners’ choice episode of Zero to Well-Read.

Spanning centuries and continents, Yaa Gyasi’s 2016 debut tracks the development and impact of slavery through nine generations of one family, from late-18th-century Africa to modern-day America.

It’s an ambitious undertaking for any writer and a truly stunning achievement for a debut. Beloved by readers, the novel ranks #21 on New York Times readers’ best books of the 21st century and has an average Goodreads rating of 4.46 stars, no easy feat.

Listen to our conversation about this now-underrated gem on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , YouTube , or wherever you find your pods. And in today’s extra credit find….

How Homecoming Came to Be 

The idea for Homegoing came to Yaa Gyasi on a writing fellowship in Ghana during the summer of her sophomore year at Stanford. One of the places she visited there was Cape Coast Castle, a trading post and slave port that held captured Africans bound for the Americas. What Gyasi learned about the African women who lived in the castle in the 18th century, including that not all of them were enslaved, inspired her to write a story that gave a voice to these women. 

Read more in this Carnegie Foundation profile of Gyasi, who was named a Great Immigrants, Great Americans honoree in 2020, then learn more about Cape Coast Castle and its role in the Transatlantic Slave Trade.

Reviewed, Times Two

items.title: The Best Books Out This Month to Read With Your Book Club
items.summary:
We’re hitting the time of year when book clubs may start to slow down, or even go on hiatus. I reckon this is because many book clubs—at least, the ones I’ve been a part of—tend to meet at the end of every month, and the end of November on till the end of the year can be tricky. For book clubs that do follow the end-of-the-month schedule, I would recommend simply having one last meeting of the year, either the first or second week of December, then resuming in early or late January. February may even be better for actual book discussion meetings, considering January’s holidays and new semesters starting. If you do meet in January, I think the meeting would be better for setting plans for the new year.

No matter what you decide to do with November (and the rest of the year), there are still great, book club-friendly books coming out this month that you’ll want to keep in mind for future discussions. They follow Irish families in the 1960s, Bangladeshi women who survive the unthinkable, the life of a Black Medici heir in Renaissance-era Florence, and more.

 Keane’s latest starts in 1960s Ireland when a tragedy splits 11 grieving sons between England and the US to survive. But then one of them goes missing.

items.title: How to Teach Information Literacy
items.summary:
The first time I learned I was allowed to disagree with a text, I was already in college. I didn’t have a library or librarians in the K-12 schools I attended and was encouraged to accept a text’s authority as absolute. If it was printed, it was true, and it never occurred to me to ask who wrote it or why. Learning to question what I read changed everything, but by then I’d lost years I could have spent practicing.

So now that I’m the librarian I never had, I’m determined that my students will know what information literacy is long before stepping foot on a college campus or out in the workforce. They’re growing up in feeds full of confident videos, polished websites, and chatbots that never show their sources, and much of it was built by someone who wants something from them. A student who knows how to question what they’ve been handed is a student who’s harder to manipulate.

The good news is that this kind of thinking can be taught. It starts with one simple habit: before deciding whether something is true, ask questions about who or where this information is from.

What is Information Literacy? 

Information literacy sounds like jargon, but the idea is simple. The Association of College and Research Libraries (ACRL) defines it as “the set of integrated abilities encompassing the reflective discovery of information, the understanding of how information is produced and valued, and the use of information in creating new knowledge and participating ethically in communities of learning.”

In other words, it means knowing how to find information thoughtfully, understanding…

items.title: LGBTQ Books to Vote for in the 2026 Goodreads Choice Awards
items.summary:
It’s that time again: the Goodreads Choice Awards . Of all the year-end best-of lists, this one is the most transparently a popularity contest. Every year, the initial round has at least some interesting choices, including—usually—queer and BIPOC representation. And every year, by the end, most of those interesting and diverse choices are gone. But hope springs eternal, and that’s why I’m sharing with you the queer books included in the opening round, so you can cast your vote and help them out. The representation of queer books has dropped in almost every category since last year, so these nominees could definitely use the boost.

Goodreads is owned by Amazon, so there’s plenty of good reasons not to support it, but the Goodreads Choice Awards are a big deal for authors, especially marginalized authors. 

Hot take: I have no shame in voting for books I haven’t read in the Goodreads Choice Awards. Almost no one has read every book in a category, so it’s already wildly skewed towards the most popular books—which usually means the books with the biggest marketing budgets. Diverse books have the deck stacked against them, so if I haven’t read a great book in that category, I always vote for the queer and BIPOC books I’ve heard good things about, even if I haven’t read them. But I’ll leave that to your discretion. Whether you’re voting for them or not, this is a good snapshot of the buzziest queer books this year.

These are just the books I immediately recognized as queer; it’s likely I missed some.

items.title: Queer Magical Realist & Fabulist Books
items.summary:
Rachel Calnek-Sugin is the author of Universe of Grace , out today from Henry Holt & Co. Below, she recommends three of her favorite queer magical realist/fabulist books. 

I’ve loved magical realism and fabulism for pretty much as long as I’ve been a reader. I devoured endless YA series—some of which had so many volumes that they took up an entire shelf of my middle school library—where otherwise normal teenage girls at boring suburban high schools had powers that made popular kids very sorry they’d ever teased them, or who spent their nights falling in love with the hot ghost who lived in their bedrooms. As I got older, I grew to love Haruki Murakami, Isabel Allende, Gabriel García Márquez, and Toni Morrison. It’s always felt right to me to read about our world—but a little magic. Because our world has always seemed at least a little magic to me. The strangest, most horrifying, most miraculous stuff happens all the time.

Lately, I’ve been reading a lot of magical realism and fabulism that also happens to be queer. Maybe it’s a bit of a golden age for this crossover? Or maybe I’m just looking for what I want to read. There’s something that feels aligned to me between queer literature and magical realism/fabulism: both suggest that other worlds are not only possible, they’re being created all the time. My new novel, Universe of Grace , is one of these books—I hope it makes readers remember that this world is profoundly weird, and that there are infinite ways for how we can live. Here are three other books that have made me feel that way.

Fruiting Bodies by Kathryn Harlan…

items.title: Belonging by Sonia Gandhi review – India’s elder stateswoman breaks her silence
items.summary:
The Italian who became kingmaker in the world’s largest democracy charts her remarkable journey

By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history.

No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi, soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years.

items.title: How to Make the Ink Used to Write Hamlet, the Declaration of Independence, and Beethoven’s Fifth
items.summary:
This is how to make the ink that wrote Magna Carta, Hamlet , Samuel Pepys’s Diary , Robinson Crusoe , Gulliver’s Travels , Candide , the Declaration of Independence, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman , Beethoven’s Fifth, Les Misérables , and everything in between. The recipe comes from the UK National Archives, written circa 1483:

To make hynke. Take gall & coporos & or vitrial quartryn & gumme of eueryche a quartryn oþer helf quartryn & a halfe quartryn of gall more & breke þe gall a ij oþer a iij & put ham togedere eueryche one in a pot & stere hyt ofte & wyƷt wythinne ij wykys after Ʒe mow wryte þer wyþ. & yf Ʒe have a quartryn of eueryche take a quarte of watyr yf halfe a quartryn of eueryche þan take half a quartre of watyr.

If that isn’t entirely clear, there are other ways. First, sit under an oak tree. Second, look for the oak galls, also known as oak apples, the hazelnut-size balls that grow when a gall wasp lays an egg within the underside of a leaf and the tree secretes tannic and gallic acids. Remove two ounces of galls, and once dried, grind them with mortar and pestle. Add a pint of water and leave for a day or two (in medieval manuals, wine and vinegar are frequent alternatives to water, being less likely to make you sick). Then strain through fine linen or gauze, and add an ounce of ferrous sulphate (the “coporos” mentioned in 1483). Now add three flakes of the fixative gum arabic (a golden-colored sap collected from acacia trees) which will also increase gloss and flow, and leave in a cool place—a windowsill is ideal—for a fortnight, stirring daily.…

items.title: How Anita Brookner Restarted Her Life at 52
items.summary:
Brookner was fifty-two (though she was soon to be ten years younger). She had a novel. She had an agent. Before long she would have a publisher. She was still teaching, and would be for some years to come, but she was changing her life. How did that happen? She told Anna Whitworth that she was writing a novel on her ancient typewriter to “fill the empty quarter,” up in her room at the Courtauld, when everyone else was away on their summer holidays. Whitworth, who knew that her friend suffered from depression, thought that novel-writing was her means of dealing with it. Brookner herself said as much, in interview after interview from the early 1980s onwards. She constructed a set-piece narrative. (This didn’t include a momentary “road not taken,” when, just after publishing David , she wrote to Chatto asking if she might write a Life of Mme de Staël: she would need a contract, as the job would involve living in Switzerland for a while. No, they replied, it wasn’t commercial enough.) She always said that when she started writing her first novel she was experiencing sadness, desperation and boredom, to the point of being “endangered.” She was “unhappy” and “alone” and “she wanted to know how she had deserved such a fate.” There was “a gap,” a lack of “structure” in her life, a need to “fill the time.”

She is never specific about details, of course, but reaching her fifties without family or children, the shock and disappointment of the Blunt scandal, her hidden feelings for MacLehose, the end of her work on David , and her increasing feeling of alienation from the way art…
items.t: How Anita Brookner Restarted Her Life at 52

items.title: Why I Had to Write My Memoir Under a Pseudonym
items.summary:
“What’s your real name, not your stripper name?”

– Lil Wayne on Juicy J’s Bandz A Make Her Dance 

*

Azra Liaqat Khan is not my name, but suppose it was:

My students might read my memoir and learn about the singularly unattractive customer who was nevertheless able to bring me to climax from the friction of a lap dance alone. They’d know that I once was trapped in a hotel room, taking a shower in front of a deranged customer in exchange for a bag of coke, and that even in my late-20’s, terrified of my parents, I spent a massive sum on trips to Charlotte, where Ammi and Abbu introduced me to the next in their line of lackluster bachelors. So much for my authoritative no-AI policy and my meticulous teaching notes.

If Azra Liaqat Khan was my real name, my university would waste no time in removing me from its list of speakers for local high school recruitment events, barred as sex workers are from contact with youth. Keynote invitations to universities would also dry up, as “Here’s the time I swindled a customer by letting him think my parents were slum dwellers in India” doesn’t quite scream Serious Political Scientist. (Despite all the handwringing about radical left professors in academia, higher ed remains a bastion of conservatism.) I’d become nothing other than Muslim-Stripper-Turned-Professor. So much for my professional reputation.

The question isn’t why I wrote Mona under a pseudonym. The question is, how else could I have written it?

If Azra Liaqat Khan was my real name, those I piss off in my book (the rightwing Indian nationalists and the religious zealots…

items.title: On Brian Blanchfield’s Proxies and the Respite of Queer Stories
items.summary:
In 2018, a new friend of mine gave me Brian Blanchfield’s Proxies with a knowing smile and a promise that I would love it. I have to admit here that this friend and I were in the early dances of a mutual crush. This is, after all, the known gifting language of any good lesbian. Give them a book filled with a spiraling narrator searching equally for knowledge and failure; give them a book filled with the gritty details of hands-free sex, even the slightest attempt at defining scissoring, a book that states, ‘We fucked, some of us, a feeling of fucking, felt for the feeling in one another, and got off on it.’

I went into Proxies blindly and of course the trick worked. Later my new friend and I would go on to make out in a snowy cab ride home, after lingering too long over glasses of orange wine at Molasses Books . But more than the queer desire that quietly colors Proxies , what captivated me most about Blachfield’s third book was his ability to weave between genre with little care for establishing parameters for his reader. Or was he able to weave between genre because of his transparency in parameters? Either way I shook it, the book read like an assured contradiction to itself. Blanchfield’s writing existed solely for his own sake. Simultaneously, it seemed to be laying new ground for how a memoir should behave.

Told through 24 short essays, Proxies combines autobiography with apparently arbitrary interest points. First published in January 2016, each essay tests the limits of writing the self. Blachfield sets out always with purpose and yet his starting point…
items.t: On Brian Blanchfield’s Proxies and the Respite of Queer Stories

items.title: Song and Spirit: On Understanding My Grandmother’s Deeply-Held Devotion
items.summary:
In the morning everyone was asleep except for Grandma and me. I lay awake in bed between my cousin Rhonda and girl-aunt Sheila, listening for Grandma to rise in the quiet dark. Knowing she liked to be alone first thing in the morning, I waited until the kettle whistled, the toilet flushed, and the oven door opened and closed before coming downstairs. The kitchen smelled of sugar, coffee, butter, and bread.

I stood in the doorway as she was in the middle of committing a Bible verse to memory.

“Nik-’em-Hick-’em-Slick-’em Ball,” she greeted me singing in her raspy alto. “Do you want toast?”

I kept my answer to a nod. Grandma didn’t like a lot of chatter first thing in the morning, and I was known around the house for asking too many questions and having too many opinions. Once I started, I got carried away, and she would say, “Oh, Nik, can you just be quiet for once? My goodness.”

I rested my head on the table while she made me breakfast, my feet barely reaching the linoleum floor. She moved about the kitchen slowly, still sipping her coffee. I picked up bits and pieces of her thoughts as she talked to herself and prepared for the day. The quieter I remained, the more she shared.

Grandma sang a funny song from her childhood. She knew I loved when she sang it in her high-pitched, playful way.

Turkey in the straw

Turkey in the straw

Roll ’em up and twist ’em up

A high tuck a-haw

And hit ’em up a tune called

Turkey in the Straw 

This she followed with funny animal sounds. A minstrel song, I would learn decades later.

“Where are my friends Bob and Joe?” she wondered,…
items.t: Song and Spirit: On Understanding My Grandmother’s Deeply-Held Devotion

items.title: The Key Biscayne Affair
items.summary:
Our problems began as soon as we touched down in Miami. Men in black vests greeted us when we disembarked. Somehow our reputation preceded us—the mysterious trio, traveling sans documentation—and we were escorted to a small room. Nico and I were ordered to sit. Our father was interrogated, then finally released when he made a call to the consulate.

On our way out of the room, they had our father pass through a metal detector. It beeped. We tried to convince the guards that he had an iron femur, but they scoffed.

“No, it’s true. They had to reconstruct his whole femur after a motorcycle accident in Barcelona,” Nico explained. “He doesn’t have a watch or a belt or any change on him. It’s his iron leg.”

Our dad stepped in and out of the metal detector, smiling, friendly, pockets turned out, eliciting beeps every time, as if he were about to bow before the astonishment of the security personnel, who stood there unmoving. It seemed like a magic trick.

“Go on, check under my clothes. But no funny business! I don’t have anything, I swear. It’s my leg. You can arrest me for piracy, though. Arr!”

The metal detector beeped again. The Miami guards’ expressions were similar to the look we’d seen on the woman behind the counter in Boston: a kind of bewilderment, one that didn’t laugh in the face of something so ridiculous—vagabond prince, pirate professor—but instead tried to reach a solution in record time. My brother tried reasoning with them, my dad kept up his circus act, and I was his devoted audience.

“What do you mean an ‘iron leg’?”

The guards called over a police…

items.title: The Brightness by Chad Harbach review – an ambitious sequel to The Art of Fielding
items.summary:
Fifteen years on, this expansive follow-up to the campus epic explores female agency, friendship – and the messiness of early adulthood

Back in 2011, Chad Harbach’s debut The Art of Fielding was hailed as the next Great American Novel. Set on the campus of Westish, a fictional midwestern liberal arts college, and steeped in baseball, it grappled with the big, quintessentially American themes – ambition, failure, the pursuit of perfection – that have traditionally been the genre’s hallmark. Harbach himself winkingly invited the categorisation: The Art of Fielding communes directly with the spirit of Herman Melville, arguably the greatest Great American Novelist of them all. Westish College, the novel explains, has claimed Melville as its own since the discovery of a lecture he gave there in 1880: its baseball team is known as the Harpooners; and a Melville statue presides over the campus like the genius of the place.

Legend has it that Harbach laboured over The Art of Fielding for more than a decade. When it finally emerged, a feverish bidding war saw it sell for more than $650,000 (£431,000), a saga chronicled at length in Vanity Fair. Any follow-up to such a high-profile debut, let alone one 15 years in the making, was always going to be read against the original. The Brightness, set on the same campus and peopled by many of the same characters, all but demands direct comparison. Throw in the fact that Harbach’s first novel actually turns up inside its…

items.title: I Want to Have a Baby Because I Miss the Violence
items.summary:
An excerpt from Nanny Nanny by K Chiucarello 

I had a feeling this was coming when Michael began texting heavily a few days ago. On the first snow of the season, he texted to say he’d had a dream about Jenny.

You know your friend Jenny? he asked me.

Jenny, as in my best friend? I replied.

Exactly, he said.

In the dream Jenny had gotten a tattoo of a tampon on the back of her leg, right in the ditch behind the knee, which I hear is one of the most painful body parts to place something permanent. Michael thought it was funny and specific that Jenny had appeared to him in the night and that a tampon was involved.

He texted, Do you remember telling me about those, about periods and the smell of rust that hits the nose when a flood opens like that?

In high school, I had been the first to teach him all about tampons. We were in his Buick when I explained to him all the chores women must suffer through when they begin their periods. There’s ruined jeans, I told him, and heating pads, long hours of lying horizontal or moving through the world with cotton shoved into you. A string. A metallic smell, I said, crinkling my poreless face. Here, I said, leaning over to Michael from the passenger seat. Smell this. And I shoved a fake gold bracelet my mother had purchased for me into his nose.

It’s certainly a smell, he replied, reclining back into the driver’s seat.

So. Michael had this dream about Jenny getting a tampon tattoo and he texted me, coming back into my life like clockwork, like he does every season.

We never could stop speaking for good, despite both of us acting,…
items.t: I Want to Have a Baby Because I Miss the Violence

items.title: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian
items.summary:
Mortimer’s off-kilter charm energises the story of a troubled teenager in 1970s Middlesbrough

In comedian Bob Mortimer’s fourth novel, Michael, when we meet him, isn’t an angel; but he’s in a place that he suspects is at least angel-adjacent. He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14.

So back down memory lane we amble, the mysterious and otherworldly frame story intruding only in brief chapters now and again, recounting our hero’s comically tetchy exchanges with Charles. Here, really, is a sweet coming-of-age story with a delicate frosting of It’s a Wonderful Life.

Continue reading...

items.title: The Sensualist by Gary Shteyngart review – a delectable romp through life’s pleasures
items.summary:
From martinis to capybara videos, the novelist celebrates the little things (some more expensive than others) that bring him joy

In 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants.

And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalization … I couldn’t make my adopted country fall out of love with fascism, but at least I could enjoy my new shoes.” Clothes become an advanced form of self-care.

Continue reading...

items.title: The unexpected power of fleeting friendships
items.summary:
From Aristotle on, we’ve learned to see long-lasting relationships as more valuable. But what does that leave out?

In Russian, a poputchik is a stranger you meet on a journey who you end up confessing everything to because you know you’ll never see them again. Like the English “fellow traveller”, poputchik was repurposed to describe Marxist sympathisers, but the original meaning intrigues me most.

The idea that we might safely unburden ourselves to strangers, or have their secrets bestowed upon us, is deeply embedded in Russian culture. It’s there in Leo Tolstoy’s The Kreutzer Sonata: as the windows tremble and the tundra passes in a hypnotic blur, Pozdnyshev tells his life story of marriage, betrayal and murder. Or in Venedikt Erofeev’s 1970s satire Moscow to the End of the Line, in which a retired cable fitter drunkenly hops a train and unfurls a sublime monologue on politics, society, love and, of course, vodka. A Russian friend jokes that this is “therapy, Soviet-style”.

Continue reading...
items.t: The unexpected power of fleeting friendships

items.title: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her
items.summary:
A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back

Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes.

“But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.

Continue reading...

items.title: 7 Books About Mothers with Voracious Interior Lives
items.summary:
The political project constraining American women, the one that gave us Dobbs , rests on a picture of motherhood as a woman’s entirety. Instinctive, total, self-abnegating, and therefore requiring no compensation, no consent, and no interior life. A reader of feminist theory may hear Silvia Federici’s “Wages Against Housework”: Housework “transformed into a natural attribute of our female physique and personality” so that it could go unpaid. “They say it is love. We say it is unwaged work.” Fifty years ago, Adrienne Rich named it the institution of motherhood—distinct from the experience—and the institution now has a legislative program foisted on us by predators. 

Every book on this list documents a mother who is also something else. Voracious. Desiring. Fixated on a dead poet, a diary, a theology, a body’s capacity for harm. Sometimes in psychosis. Sometimes distracted by thoughts which have nothing to do with the baby. The obsession is evidence of an interior life beyond motherhood, whatever its perils. 

I know this fixation from the inside. Sleepless with an infant, I became obsessed with an ancient mother goddess named Cybele, and I followed her from Galicia to the archives of the Louvre while examining my own Cuban matrilineage. The memoir that came of it is Desire Lines . 

Whether memoir, or essay, or confession, or autotheory, or hybrid of essay and autofiction, every one of these books is a mother’s account of a life that did not stop with the arrival of her child. They are literature first. Their political force follows from their craft. Propaganda simplifies…

items.title: This Cursed Beautiful Land by Evan Gershkovich review – jailed in Putin’s Russia
items.summary:
The US reporter wrongly imprisoned for espionage writes compellingly about his ordeal

Evan Gershkovich is the Wall Street Journal reporter who, in the early phase of Putin’s war in Ukraine, was snatched up by the Russian authorities on bogus espionage charges and spent a year and a half in Russian jails (first Lefortovo and then Yekaterinburg) before being released in a prisoner exchange in 2024.

The opening section of his book about the experience is gripping and rather moving. He recounts his arrest in a sting operation, after meeting a contact who promised to supply him with information about Russia’s military-industrial preparations. Born to Russian Jewish immigrant parents in the US, Gershkovich grew up in suburban New Jersey on a diet of Soviet cartoons and “Krylov’s fables rather than Aesop’s”; he was betwixt and between. When he found his way into journalism in his early 20s – first working nights as an editorial assistant at the New York Times, then getting started properly as a reporter at the Moscow Times – he gravitated to Russia and fell in love with it.
